content_voiceover: Primary CNS lymphoma is a distinct entity worth knowing cold for boards. Ninety-five percent are diffuse large B cell lymphoma, and specifically the activated B cell, or ABC, subtype, which tends to behave more aggressively than germinal center type. Median age at diagnosis is sixty. Here's a testable epidemiologic shift: incidence has actually declined in HIV positive patients thanks to antiretroviral therapy, but it's been rising in immunocompetent patients, so don't assume this is only an immunosuppression-related disease anymore. Ocular involvement matters too, intraocular lymphoma accounts for ten to twenty percent of cases, and you should always get a slit lamp exam. Sixteen percent have concurrent leptomeningeal involvement, so CSF cytology and flow cytometry are part of the workup. Extraneural, meaning systemic, disease is uncommon, only four to twelve percent, and B symptoms like fever, night sweats, and weight loss are extremely uncommon, unlike systemic DLBCL. On immunohistochemistry, BCL6 is positive in sixty to eighty percent, while CD10 positivity is much lower, only ten to twenty percent, reflecting a mostly non-germinal-center immunophenotype.
keypoints: PCNSL: 95% DLBCL, ABC subtype, median age 60
Incidence rising in immunocompetent, declining in HIV-positive patients
B symptoms extremely uncommon (unlike systemic DLBCL)
